subtopic_detail: Recognising a surgical emergency behind a common clozapine adverse effect
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 38 year old man with treatment resistant schizophrenia who has taken clozapine 450 mg daily for two years with a stable mental state. He tells you he has not opened his bowels for five days and that his belly has become tight and swollen.

He brought up dark green fluid twice this morning and has not been able to keep water down since. His abdomen is distended and tympanic with no guarding and no bowel sounds audible over two minutes. He takes an occasional docusate tablet that his mother buys for him and no other regular medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108 beats per minute, blood pressure 116/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 37.3 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 13.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), neutrophils 9.2 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), potassium 3.3 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 108 micromol/L (60-110), lactate 2.4 mmol/L (less than 2.0)
data_table.Examination: Distended tympanic abdomen with no bowel sounds and an empty rectum on digital examination

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe macrogol daily and review the bowel chart in 48 hours
options.rationale: An osmotic laxative is the right long term prophylaxis but treating an obstructed bowel as ordinary constipation is the error that makes this complication fatal in around a quarter of reported cases (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Continue clozapine and add docusate with senna each evening
options.rationale: Continuing the causative drug allows the anticholinergic and antiserotonergic effect on gut motility to persist, and a stimulant laxative in a bowel with no peristalsis risks perforation (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Reduce the clozapine dose and start a stimulant laxative today
options.rationale: Dose reduction is too slow and too partial for an acutely obstructed bowel, and imaging is required before any laxative is chosen (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Withhold clozapine and arrange an urgent abdominal radiograph
options.rationale: Absent bowel sounds with distension, vomiting and a rising lactate indicate clozapine induced gastrointestinal hypomotility progressing to ileus, which needs the drug withheld, urgent imaging and surgical involvement (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Arrange an outpatient colonoscopy within the next two weeks
options.rationale: Colonoscopy investigates mucosal disease and is contraindicated in suspected obstruction because of perforation risk, whereas the problem here is motility rather than a luminal lesion (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia).

explanation.summary: Clozapine induced gastrointestinal hypomotility is more lethal than agranulocytosis yet attracts none of the mandated monitoring, because the drug has potent anticholinergic and serotonin antagonist effects that slow colonic transit by around fourfold. Constipation affects up to 60 per cent of patients and progresses in a minority to faecal impaction, ileus, ischaemia, perforation and death. Patients often do not report symptoms because of reduced interoceptive awareness and negative symptoms, so bowel habit must be asked about at every review rather than waited for. Australian practice is to start prophylactic laxatives at initiation for anyone with risk factors and to treat any patient with abdominal distension and absent bowel sounds as a surgical emergency until imaging proves otherwise.
key_points: Gastrointestinal hypomotility causes more clozapine deaths than agranulocytosis
Patients frequently under report bowel symptoms so they must be asked about routinely
Absent bowel sounds with distension is an emergency, not simple constipation
Withhold clozapine and image before choosing any laxative
Prophylactic osmotic laxatives are recommended from initiation in at risk patients
explanation.pearls: Anticholinergic drugs such as benztropine, and opioids, multiply the risk of clozapine induced ileus, so review the whole medication chart for these before restarting clozapine once the obstruction has resolved.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: Antidepressant associated inappropriate antidiuresis in an older adult
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 79 year old woman who started sertraline 50 mg daily four weeks ago for a moderate depressive episode. Her daughter says she has become sleepy in the afternoons, is unsteady getting out of her chair, and twice this week could not remember the day.

Her mood and appetite had begun to improve before this change. Her mucous membranes are moist, her jugular venous pressure is visible 2 cm above the sternal angle and there is no peripheral oedema or postural drop. She takes no diuretic and her serum sodium was 139 mmol/L before the antidepressant was started.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 124 mmol/L (135-145), serum osmolality 258 mmol/kg (275-295), urine osmolality 480 mmol/kg, urine sodium 62 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90)
data_table.Additional tests: Thyroid stimulating hormone and 9 am cortisol within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue sertraline and restrict oral fluid to 1000 mL daily
options.rationale: Fluid restriction alone leaves the causative drug in place, and in an older woman with impaired thirst it is often poorly tolerated and only partially effective (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Switch to citalopram and recheck the serum sodium in one week
options.rationale: All selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors carry this risk as a class effect, so switching within the class invites recurrence, and citalopram adds QT prolongation in this age group (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Commence tolvaptan and continue the current antidepressant
options.rationale: A vasopressin receptor antagonist is reserved for persistent inappropriate antidiuresis with no removable cause, and using it here treats the consequence while leaving the trigger untouched (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Infuse hypertonic 3 per cent sodium chloride 100 mL over 10 minutes
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline boluses are for seizures or a substantially depressed conscious state, and using them for intermittent disorientation risks overcorrection and osmotic demyelination (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Cease sertraline and restrict oral fluid with sodium recheck
options.rationale: A euvolaemic hypo osmolar hyponatraemia with concentrated urine, normal thyroid and adrenal function and a temporal link to a new serotonergic drug is drug induced inappropriate antidiuresis, treated by stopping the drug with fluid restriction and monitoring (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors cause hyponatraemia by promoting antidiuretic hormone release, and the risk is concentrated in the first four weeks of treatment and in older, female and low weight patients. The presentation is easy to misattribute because lethargy, unsteadiness and poor concentration overlap with both depression itself and normal ageing, so a sodium level before and a few weeks after starting is prudent in anyone over 65. Diagnosis requires demonstrating euvolaemia with a low serum osmolality, an inappropriately concentrated urine and a urine sodium above 30 mmol per litre, with thyroid and adrenal causes excluded. If an antidepressant remains necessary, agents with a lower reported risk such as mirtazapine or agomelatine are preferred, with the sodium rechecked two weeks after restarting.
key_points: Risk is highest in the first four weeks of an antidepressant in older patients
Symptoms overlap with depression itself, so check the sodium rather than assume
Diagnosis requires euvolaemia, low serum osmolality and concentrated urine
The risk is a class effect, so switching within the class often recurs
Mirtazapine carries a lower reported risk if an antidepressant is still needed
explanation.pearls: Check the serum sodium two weeks after starting or increasing any antidepressant in a patient over 65 years, because most drug induced hyponatraemia appears within the first month and is asymptomatic until it is severe.

subtopic_detail: Choosing first line management for behavioural symptoms where antipsychotic sensitivity is expected
stem:
You are the general practitioner asked to review a 78 year old man in residential aged care whose cognition has declined over three years. Staff describe days when he converses normally and days when he stares and cannot be roused into conversation, and he regularly tells them there are children standing in the corner of his room.

His wife says he shouts and kicks in his sleep and has fallen out of bed twice. He has a stooped posture and slow movements without a tremor. For the past two weeks he has been shouting and pushing staff away during evening personal care, and no trigger has been identified.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 70 beats per minute, blood pressure 126/74 mmHg lying, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium, liver function tests, thyroid stimulating hormone, urinalysis and chest radiograph within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 4 mg daily and colecalciferol 1000 units daily, with no changes in six months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Commence risperidone 0.5 mg twice daily and review in one week
options.rationale: Fluctuating cognition, formed visual hallucinations, dream enactment and parkinsonism indicate a synucleinopathy, in which up to half of patients have severe sensitivity reactions to antipsychotics with rigidity and a sharp rise in mortality (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Implement a behaviour support plan and review pain and constipation
options.rationale: Non pharmacological measures with a systematic search for unrecognised pain, constipation and environmental triggers are first line for behavioural symptoms in dementia, and are especially important here because antipsychotics are hazardous in this subtype (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Dementia Australia).

options.text: Commence haloperidol 0.5 mg as required for episodes of agitation
options.rationale: A high potency typical antipsychotic carries the greatest risk of a severe sensitivity reaction in this group and is specifically avoided (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence olanzapine 2.5 mg each night and review again in one week
options.rationale: Olanzapine has substantial anticholinergic activity that worsens cognition and hallucinations in this subtype, and it shares the class risk of stroke and death in dementia (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence diazepam 2 mg twice daily and review again in one week
options.rationale: A long acting benzodiazepine accumulates in older people and causes falls, sedation and paradoxical disinhibition, and it is not a first line treatment for behavioural symptoms in dementia (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Behavioural and psychological symptoms affect most people with dementia at some point and are the commonest reason antipsychotics are prescribed in residential care, despite an absolute increase in mortality and stroke and only modest benefit. Australian practice requires a structured search for unmet needs first, covering pain, constipation, urinary retention, infection, sensory impairment, boredom and the manner in which personal care is delivered, since resistance during care is very often pain related. Recognising the dementia subtype changes the risk calculation sharply, because dementia with Lewy bodies brings severe antipsychotic sensitivity reactions with rigidity, autonomic instability and death. When drug treatment does become necessary in that subtype, a cholinesterase inhibitor such as rivastigmine is preferred and quetiapine or clozapine are the only antipsychotics considered.
key_points: Fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, dream enactment and parkinsonism define the subtype
Up to half of these patients have severe antipsychotic sensitivity reactions
Search systematically for pain, constipation, infection and care delivery triggers
Antipsychotics increase stroke and mortality in all forms of dementia
Cholinesterase inhibitors are preferred if drug treatment becomes necessary in this subtype
explanation.pearls: A time limited analgesic trial with regular paracetamol 1 g three times daily for two weeks reduces agitation in residential care residents with dementia, and is a safer first drug step than any psychotropic.

subtopic_detail: Managing an elevated mood state caused by a drug that cannot simply be stopped
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the respiratory ward about a 58 year old man on day five of prednisolone 50 mg daily for an exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Nursing staff say he has not slept for two nights, talks over everyone, and telephoned his sister at three in the morning about buying a caravan to drive around the country.

He is irritable when interrupted but knows where he is, follows a three step command and can recite the months backwards. He sees and hears nothing unusual. He has no psychiatric history and no family history of mood disorder, and he is still wheezy with an oxygen requirement of 2 litres per minute.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 142/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 93 per cent on 2 litres per minute, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium, liver function tests, thyroid stimulating hormone and urinalysis within normal limits, blood glucose 9.2 mmol/L (3.0-7.7 fasting)
data_table.Substance history: No alcohol for six years, no illicit substance use, urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reduce prednisolone to the lowest effective dose and add olanzapine
options.rationale: Corticosteroid induced mood elevation is dose related, so the first move is to lower the dose as far as the airways disease allows, with a short course of an antipsychotic to control the elevated state while that happens (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Commence lithium and continue prednisolone at the current dose
options.rationale: Lithium takes one to two weeks to act, requires monitoring and carries interaction risks, and leaving the corticosteroid dose unchanged means the driver of the episode persists (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Commence sodium valproate and continue prednisolone unchanged
options.rationale: Valproate is a reasonable alternative antimanic drug but the same objection applies, since treating the episode without addressing the cause prolongs it unnecessarily (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Continue prednisolone and prescribe temazepam for the insomnia
options.rationale: Treating the insomnia in isolation mislabels an elevated mood state as a sleep problem, and a hypnotic will not control the pressured speech, irritability or disinhibited spending (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Cease prednisolone abruptly and commence sertraline for the mood
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after several days of high dose corticosteroid risks both an airways relapse and adrenal insufficiency, and an antidepressant would worsen rather than treat an elevated mood state (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Psychiatric reactions occur in around 5 to 6 per cent of patients given high dose corticosteroids, with risk rising steeply above a prednisolone equivalent of 40 mg daily. Elevated or mixed states predominate in the first weeks, while depressive presentations are commoner with prolonged therapy, and the onset is typically within the first five days. The key clinical discrimination is from delirium, which is why preserved orientation, attention and the absence of perceptual disturbance are documented explicitly. Management balances two competing needs: the psychiatric episode responds to dose reduction, while the underlying condition may still require the drug, so the dose is minimised rather than stopped and a short course of an antipsychotic covers the interval. A past corticosteroid induced episode does not preclude future treatment but does warrant prophylaxis and closer observation.
key_points: Risk rises sharply above prednisolone 40 mg daily and onset is usually within five days
Elevated and mixed states predominate early, depressive states with prolonged use
Preserved attention and orientation separate this from delirium
Reduce the corticosteroid dose rather than stopping it abruptly
Antidepressants can worsen a corticosteroid induced elevated mood state
explanation.pearls: Olanzapine 5 to 10 mg daily typically controls corticosteroid induced mood elevation within days and can be withdrawn once the corticosteroid dose falls below a prednisolone equivalent of 20 mg daily.

subtopic_detail: Selecting pharmacotherapy where one antidepressant class is specifically contraindicated
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24 year old woman who has been binge eating and then making herself vomit about four times a week for two years. She has been seeing a psychologist fortnightly for three months and finds the sessions useful but says the urges are still overwhelming.

For the past two months she has also had persistently low mood, poor concentration and early morning waking. Her body mass index is 22 kg per square metre and her blood pressure shows no postural drop. She has never had a seizure, takes no regular medication and asks whether a tablet could help.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 68 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), bicarbonate 30 mmol/L (22-32), magnesium 0.78 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), full blood count and liver function tests within normal limits
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Sinus rhythm with a corrected QT interval of 424 ms

lead_in: Which medication is the most appropriate addition?

options.text: Commence bupropion 150 mg daily alongside psychological therapy
options.rationale: Bupropion is contraindicated in current or past purging disorders because the seizure rate in that group is far higher than in the general population (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Commence topiramate 50 mg daily alongside psychological therapy
options.rationale: Topiramate reduces binge frequency in trials but causes weight loss and cognitive adverse effects, so it is a later line option rather than the first medication offered (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Eating Disorders Guideline).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Eating Disorders Guideline

options.text: Commence fluoxetine 60 mg daily alongside psychological therapy
options.rationale: Fluoxetine at 60 mg daily is the only antidepressant with established efficacy for reducing binge and purge frequency in bulimia nervosa and it also treats the comorbid depressive episode (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Eating Disorders Guideline; Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Eating Disorders Guideline

options.text: Commence mirtazapine 30 mg daily alongside psychological therapy
options.rationale: Mirtazapine has no trial evidence in bulimia nervosa and its appetite stimulating effect is likely to increase binge frequency (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Eating Disorders Guideline).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Eating Disorders Guideline

options.text: Commence venlafaxine 75 mg daily alongside psychological therapy
options.rationale: Venlafaxine treats the depression but has no established antibulimic effect, and the distinguishing point is that the benefit of fluoxetine is specific to that drug rather than a class effect (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Eating Disorders Guideline).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Eating Disorders Guideline

explanation.summary: Psychological therapy remains first line for bulimia nervosa, with eating disorder focused cognitive behavioural therapy having the strongest evidence, and medication is an adjunct rather than a substitute. Fluoxetine is the exception among antidepressants in that the dose used for bulimia is higher than the antidepressant dose and the antibulimic effect appears independent of any change in mood. Physical monitoring matters alongside the psychiatric treatment because recurrent vomiting causes hypokalaemia, a metabolic alkalosis, dental erosion and parotid swelling, and hypokalaemia is the finding that most often leads to hospital admission. Medication is not started in place of therapy, and a lack of response at eight to twelve weeks prompts review of the therapy rather than escalation of the drug.
key_points: Eating disorder focused cognitive behavioural therapy is first line treatment
Fluoxetine 60 mg daily is the only antidepressant with proven antibulimic effect
Bupropion is contraindicated because of seizure risk in purging disorders
Recurrent vomiting causes hypokalaemia with a metabolic alkalosis
The antibulimic effect of fluoxetine is independent of its antidepressant effect
explanation.pearls: The antibulimic dose of fluoxetine is 60 mg daily, three times the usual starting antidepressant dose, and patients should be told to expect a reduction in binge frequency within three to four weeks of reaching that dose.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Eating Disorders Guideline
